title: High-risk chest pain features
text:
Chest pain described as pressure, tightness, or heaviness — especially if it radiates to the left
arm, jaw, or back, or is accompanied by sweating, nausea, or breathlessness — should be treated as
a possible cardiac emergency and referred immediately to the nearest hospital with emergency care.

title: Immediate steps while arranging transport
citation: chest_pain_cardiac § Immediate steps while arranging transport
text:
Keep the patient calm and seated or in a comfortable half-reclined position. Loosen tight clothing.
Do not make the patient walk unnecessarily or exert themselves. Arrange the fastest available
transport to a hospital or CHC with emergency capability; do not wait to see if the pain resolves.

title: Lower-risk chest discomfort
text:
Sharp, brief chest pain that changes with body position or breathing, without sweating,
radiation, or breathlessness, is less likely to be cardiac in origin but should still be assessed
by a Sub-Centre or ANM if it persists, to rule out other causes.

title: Unconsciousness or convulsions
text:
A patient who is unconscious, unusually drowsy and hard to wake, or has convulsions (fits/seizures)
needs immediate emergency referral to the nearest hospital or CHC. Do not attempt to give anything
by mouth. Keep the patient on their side to prevent choking, and arrange transport immediately.

title: Inability to drink or feed
citation: danger_signs § Inability to drink or feed
text:
A patient who is unable to drink or breastfeed, or who vomits everything they are given, is showing
a danger sign and needs urgent referral. This applies especially to infants and young children.

title: Severe bleeding
text:
Any severe or uncontrolled bleeding, from any site, is an emergency. Apply firm direct pressure to
the bleeding site with a clean cloth while arranging immediate transport to the nearest facility with
surgical/emergency capability.

title: Blue or grey skin color (cyanosis)
citation: danger_signs § Blue or grey skin color (cyanosis)
text:
Bluish or greyish discoloration of the lips, tongue, or skin indicates the body is not getting enough
oxygen. This is always an emergency requiring immediate referral, regardless of other symptoms.

title: Severe chest indrawing or grunting (children)
citation: danger_signs § Severe chest indrawing or grunting (children)
text:
In young children, the chest wall pulling in sharply with each breath, or audible grunting sounds
while breathing, indicates severe respiratory distress and needs immediate referral.

title: Falls in the elderly
text:
A fall in an elderly person, even without obvious injury, warrants careful assessment — check for
inability to stand/walk normally, severe pain, confusion, or head injury. Any of these needs
referral, as older adults are at higher risk of fractures and internal injury from falls.

title: Confusion or sudden behavior change
citation: elderly_care § Confusion or sudden behavior change
text:
Sudden new confusion, drowsiness, or agitation in an elderly person can indicate an underlying
infection (e.g. urinary tract infection), medication side effect, dehydration, or a more serious
condition like stroke. This is not a normal part of aging and should be assessed promptly rather
than dismissed.

title: Managing multiple chronic conditions
text:
Many elderly patients take multiple medications for chronic conditions. Encourage them to keep an
up-to-date list of all medications and bring it to every health visit, and to never stop a
prescribed medication without medical advice.

title: Pressure sores (bedsores)
text:
In bedridden elderly patients, check regularly for red or broken skin over bony areas (heels,
hips, lower back). Reposition the patient every 2 hours where possible, and keep skin clean and
dry. Refer if a sore is deep, infected, or not healing.

title: Assessing fever severity
text:
A fever alone, without other danger signs, is usually manageable at home or with a Sub-Centre/ANM
visit. Fever accompanied by lethargy, inability to feed, convulsions, or persistent high fever
(above 102°F / 39°C) for more than 2-3 days should be referred for further assessment.

title: Home care for mild fever
citation: fever_and_dehydration § Home care for mild fever
text:
Keep the patient in a cool, well-ventilated area. Encourage plenty of fluids (water, buttermilk,
coconut water). Use a damp cloth to sponge the skin if the fever feels very high. Monitor
temperature and general alertness over the next 24 hours.

title: Signs of dehydration
text:
Look for: sunken eyes, dry mouth/tongue, reduced or dark urine, skin that stays pinched when
gently pulled (poor skin turgor), and unusual thirst or lethargy. Any of these signs, especially
in a child, indicate at least moderate dehydration.

title: Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS)
text:
For diarrhea, vomiting, or suspected dehydration without danger signs, give ORS solution
frequently in small sips — roughly one cup after every loose stool for an adult, or a few spoonfuls
every few minutes for an infant. Continue feeding/breastfeeding as normal alongside ORS. If the
patient cannot keep ORS down, or dehydration signs worsen, refer to the Sub-Centre or CHC.

title: Assessing severity
text:
Frequent vomiting or watery diarrhea (several episodes within a few hours), especially combined
with dehydration signs (sunken eyes, poor skin turgor, lethargy) or blood in the stool, needs
prompt referral to a Sub-Centre or CHC.

title: Home management (no danger signs)
text:
Continue ORS and normal feeding/breastfeeding. Avoid stopping food intake — small, frequent meals
are better tolerated than large ones. Monitor the frequency of loose stools/vomiting and watch
for dehydration signs over the next 12-24 hours.

title: Referral criteria
text:
Refer if: the patient cannot keep any fluids down, there is blood in vomit or stool, symptoms
persist beyond 24-48 hours without improvement, or any dehydration or other danger sign appears.

title: Cold and mild sore throat
citation: home_care_mild_symptoms § Cold and mild sore throat
text:
Warm saline gargles (a pinch of salt in warm water), steam inhalation, and plenty of warm fluids
help relieve mild cold and sore throat symptoms. These are self-limiting and generally resolve
within a few days without needing referral.

title: Mild body ache or tiredness
citation: home_care_mild_symptoms § Mild body ache or tiredness
text:
Rest, hydration, and monitoring are usually sufficient for mild, generalized body ache or
tiredness without fever or other symptoms. Encourage the patient to report if new symptoms
develop or existing ones worsen.

title: When mild symptoms need reassessment
citation: home_care_mild_symptoms § When mild symptoms need reassessment
text:
If a "mild" case develops fever above 102°F, breathing difficulty, persistent vomiting, or any
general danger sign, reassess and refer according to the relevant protocol rather than continuing
home care alone.

title: Routine childhood immunization
text:
Encourage caregivers to complete the full immunization schedule on time (BCG, OPV, DPT/pentavalent,
measles-rubella, and boosters as per the national schedule). Mild fever or soreness at the
injection site after vaccination is normal and can be managed with rest and fluids; a very high
fever, persistent crying, swelling, or a fit after vaccination should be reported and assessed.

title: Missed doses
text:
A missed or delayed vaccine dose does not mean starting the schedule over — advise catching up on
missed doses at the next available session rather than skipping them.

title: Family planning counseling
text:
Provide accurate information on available family planning methods and refer to a health worker or
facility for method selection based on the individual's health and preferences. Respect the
person's choice and avoid pressuring any particular method.

title: Adolescent health
text:
Adolescents may be hesitant to discuss health concerns openly. Create a private, non-judgmental
space for conversation, and refer concerns about growth, nutrition, menstrual health, or mental
health to the appropriate health worker.

title: Minor cuts and wounds
text:
Clean the wound with clean water and mild soap, remove visible dirt, and cover with a clean
dressing. Watch for signs of infection (increasing redness, swelling, warmth, pus, or fever) over
the following days.

title: Severe bleeding wounds
text:
Apply firm, direct pressure with a clean cloth and keep the injured part elevated if possible. Do
not remove an embedded object — stabilize it in place and refer immediately. Severe or
uncontrolled bleeding is always an emergency.

title: Burns
text:
Cool a burn immediately with clean, cool (not ice-cold) running water for at least 10-20 minutes.
Do not apply toothpaste, oil, or other home remedies. Cover loosely with a clean, non-stick
dressing. Refer to a facility if the burn is large, deep, on the face/hands/genitals, or shows
signs of infection.

title: Suspected fractures
text:
Immobilize the injured limb in the position found using a splint or firm support, and avoid
moving the patient unnecessarily. Refer to a facility with X-ray/orthopedic capability, especially
if there is visible deformity, inability to bear weight, or the bone is exposed.

title: Head injury
text:
Any head injury with loss of consciousness (even brief), repeated vomiting, confusion, unequal
pupil size, or a fit needs immediate referral for emergency assessment.

title: Recognizing severe acute malnutrition (SAM)
text:
Visible severe wasting (very thin arms/legs, loose skin folds), bilateral pitting edema (swelling)
of both feet, or a mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) below the severe threshold for age are signs
of severe acute malnutrition. These children need urgent referral to a nutrition rehabilitation
facility or hospital, as they are at high risk of complications.

title: Moderate acute malnutrition (MAM)
text:
Children who are thin but without the severe danger signs above may be managed with supplementary
feeding and close growth monitoring at the Sub-Centre/Anganwadi level, with referral if they do not
improve or develop danger signs.

title: General feeding advice
text:
Encourage age-appropriate feeding: exclusive breastfeeding until 6 months, then timely introduction
of nutrient-dense complementary foods alongside continued breastfeeding up to 2 years. Frequent
small meals are better tolerated by malnourished children than large infrequent ones.

title: When to refer immediately
text:
Any malnourished child who also shows danger signs (unable to feed, lethargy, convulsions, severe
dehydration, or breathing difficulty) needs emergency referral regardless of the malnutrition
grading above.

title: Danger signs during pregnancy
text:
Severe headache with blurred vision, swelling of the face/hands, high blood pressure, vaginal
bleeding, severe abdominal pain, reduced or absent fetal movement, high fever, or convulsions in a
pregnant woman are all emergencies requiring immediate referral to a facility with obstetric care.

title: Labor danger signs
text:
Prolonged labor (more than 12 hours), heavy bleeding before or after delivery, retained placenta,
cord prolapse, or the baby not descending normally all require urgent referral to a hospital with
delivery/surgical capability.

title: Postpartum danger signs
text:
Heavy bleeding after delivery (soaking more than one pad per hour), high fever, foul-smelling
vaginal discharge, severe abdominal pain, or convulsions within 6 weeks after delivery are
emergencies requiring immediate referral.

title: Routine antenatal care
text:
Encourage regular antenatal check-ups, iron/folic acid supplementation as prescribed by a health
worker, tetanus immunization per schedule, and a balanced diet. Advise the woman to plan delivery
at a health facility rather than at home where possible.

title: Recognizing distress
text:
Persistent sadness, withdrawal from usual activities, significant changes in sleep or appetite, or
expressions of hopelessness lasting more than two weeks may indicate depression or another mental
health concern. Approach with empathy, listen without judgment, and encourage the person to seek
support from a health worker or counselor.

title: Signs requiring urgent attention
text:
Any expression of wanting to end their life, thoughts of suicide, intent to harm oneself or
others, or a specific plan to do so, is a mental health emergency. Do not leave the person alone,
remove access to obvious means of harm if safe to do so, and arrange urgent referral to a facility
with mental health support.

title: Acute agitation or confusion
text:
Sudden severe confusion, agitation, or hallucinations — especially with fever, head injury, or in
someone with a known chronic illness — may have an underlying physical cause and needs prompt
medical assessment rather than being assumed to be purely psychological.

title: Supporting caregivers
text:
Caregivers of chronically ill or disabled family members are also at risk of stress and burnout.
Encourage they seek support for themselves as well, and connect them with community resources
where available.

title: Newborn danger signs
text:
Any of the following in a baby under 28 days old needs immediate referral: not feeding at all,
convulsions, very fast or very slow breathing, severe chest indrawing, temperature that feels very
hot or very cold to touch, yellow discoloration of skin/eyes (jaundice) especially in the first 24
hours or spreading to arms/legs, or the baby is unusually floppy or unresponsive.

title: Cord care
text:
Keep the umbilical cord stump clean and dry. Do not apply any substances, oils, or powders to the
cord. Fold the diaper below the cord stump. Seek care if the cord area becomes red, swollen, or
starts discharging pus or has a foul smell.

title: Warmth and breastfeeding
text:
Keep the newborn warm with skin-to-skin contact and appropriate wrapping, especially in the first
hours after birth. Encourage exclusive breastfeeding from within the first hour of life, with no
other foods or liquids for the first six months, unless a health worker advises otherwise.

title: Low birth weight babies
text:
Babies born very small or premature need extra warmth (skin-to-skin/kangaroo care), more frequent
breastfeeding, and closer monitoring for danger signs. Refer for specialist newborn care if
available.

title: Hypertension danger signs
text:
A known hypertensive patient with severe headache, chest pain, confusion, blurred vision, or
difficulty speaking may be having a hypertensive emergency or stroke and needs immediate referral.
Routine elevated blood pressure without these symptoms should still be followed up with an ANM or
doctor for medication review.

title: Diabetes danger signs
text:
Signs of very high blood sugar include excessive thirst, frequent urination, confusion, rapid
breathing, or a fruity-smelling breath — these need urgent referral. Signs of very low blood sugar
(common in patients on diabetes medication) include sudden sweating, shakiness, confusion, or
loss of consciousness; if the patient is conscious and able to swallow, give a sugary drink or food
immediately while arranging transport.

title: Stroke warning signs (F.A.S.T.)
text:
Face drooping on one side, Arm weakness on one side, Speech difficulty or slurring, and Time to
call for emergency transport immediately — any one of these signs, even if it resolves quickly,
needs urgent hospital assessment.

title: General chronic disease follow-up
text:
Encourage patients with known hypertension, diabetes, or heart disease to continue their prescribed
medications and attend regular follow-up visits, rather than stopping treatment when they feel
well.

title: When to refer to a District Hospital / CHC immediately (Red)
citation: referral_criteria § When to refer to a District Hospital / CHC immediately (Red)
text:
Any general danger sign (unconsciousness, convulsions, inability to drink/feed, severe bleeding,
cyanosis, severe chest indrawing), suspected cardiac emergency, or severe respiratory distress
warrants immediate referral to a facility with emergency and, where possible, ambulance capability.

title: When a Sub-Centre / ANM visit within 24 hours is appropriate (Yellow)
citation: referral_criteria § When a Sub-Centre / ANM visit within 24 hours is appropriate (Yellow)
text:
Persistent fever without danger signs, moderate dehydration responding to ORS, mild-to-moderate
breathlessness without red-flag features, or symptoms that are not improving after a day of home
care are appropriately managed with a Sub-Centre or ANM assessment rather than an emergency
referral.

title: When home care and monitoring is sufficient (Green)
citation: referral_criteria § When home care and monitoring is sufficient (Green)
text:
Mild, self-limiting symptoms — a mild cold, sore throat, or low-grade fever without any danger
signs — can usually be managed at home with rest, fluids, and monitoring, with a follow-up if
symptoms worsen or do not resolve within a few days.

title: Recognizing breathing difficulty
text:
Fast breathing, visible effort with each breath, chest indrawing, wheezing, or the patient
struggling to speak full sentences due to breathlessness are all signs of respiratory distress.
This is considered a high-risk symptom, particularly when it comes on suddenly or is worsening.

title: When it is an emergency (Red)
citation: respiratory_distress § When it is an emergency (Red)
text:
Severe breathlessness at rest, chest indrawing, grunting, blue/grey lips or skin, or breathlessness
combined with chest pain or altered consciousness require immediate emergency referral and
transport to a facility capable of oxygen support.

title: Moderate respiratory symptoms (Yellow)
text:
Mild breathlessness that improves with rest, a persistent cough without other danger signs, or
breathlessness in a patient with a known chronic condition (like asthma) who has their usual
inhaler available may be manageable with ANM/Sub-Centre assessment within a few hours, with close
monitoring for worsening.

title: First-aid while arranging transport
text:
Keep the patient sitting upright rather than lying flat, loosen tight clothing, and keep them calm.
Do not give food or water if breathlessness is severe, due to choking risk.

title: Common skin infections
text:
Redness, warmth, swelling, and pus in a localized area of skin suggest a bacterial skin infection.
Keep the area clean and dry, and refer if the redness is spreading rapidly, the patient has fever,
or the area is very painful — these suggest a more serious infection needing prompt attention.

title: Scabies and lice
text:
Intense itching, especially at night, with small burrows or bumps between fingers, wrists, or waist
suggests scabies. This is manageable with treatment from a health worker; encourage treating all
household members simultaneously and washing bedding/clothing to prevent reinfection.

title: Conjunctivitis (red eye)
text:
Redness, discharge, and irritation in one or both eyes without vision loss is usually simple
conjunctivitis. Advise gentle cleaning with clean water and avoiding touching/rubbing the eyes.
Refer if there is significant pain, vision changes, marked light sensitivity, or the discharge
persists beyond a few days.

title: Eye injury or foreign body
citation: skin_and_eye_infections § Eye injury or foreign body
text:
Do not attempt to remove an embedded foreign object from the eye. Cover loosely and refer
immediately. Any chemical splash to the eye should be rinsed with clean water for several minutes
before urgent referral.

title: Snake bite first aid
text:
Keep the patient calm and still to slow venom spread. Immobilize the bitten limb, keeping it below
heart level if possible. Remove tight clothing/jewellery near the bite before swelling starts. Do
NOT cut the wound, apply a tourniquet, try to suck out venom, or apply ice. Arrange immediate
transport to a facility that stocks anti-snake-venom.

title: Danger signs after a snake bite
citation: snake_bite_and_poisoning § Danger signs after a snake bite
text:
Difficulty breathing, drooping eyelids or blurred vision, difficulty swallowing, bleeding from
gums/nose, dark urine, or spreading swelling are all signs of severe envenomation requiring
emergency transport, even if the patient initially looks well.

title: Suspected poisoning (ingestion)
text:
Identify what was ingested if possible and bring the container/substance to the facility. Do not
induce vomiting unless specifically advised by a health professional, as some substances cause
more harm coming back up. Keep the patient calm and arrange immediate transport.

title: Insect and scorpion stings
text:
Most insect stings can be managed with a cold compress and monitoring. Refer immediately if there
is difficulty breathing, facial/throat swelling, widespread rash, or dizziness — these may indicate
a severe allergic reaction.

title: Recognizing possible TB
text:
Cough lasting more than 2 weeks, especially with blood-streaked sputum, unexplained weight loss,
persistent low-grade fever (often worse in the evening), and night sweats are classic warning signs
of pulmonary tuberculosis. Any patient with these symptoms should be referred for sputum testing or
chest X-ray at the earliest opportunity.

title: Referral and testing
text:
Refer suspected TB cases to the nearest facility offering free TB testing (sputum microscopy or
molecular testing) under the national TB program. Early diagnosis significantly improves outcomes
and reduces transmission risk to household members.

title: Supporting a diagnosed TB patient
citation: tuberculosis § Supporting a diagnosed TB patient
text:
Encourage strict adherence to the full course of treatment, even after symptoms improve, since
incomplete treatment risks drug-resistant TB. Advise good ventilation at home and covering the
mouth while coughing to reduce household transmission risk.

title: When TB symptoms become an emergency
citation: tuberculosis § When TB symptoms become an emergency
text:
Coughing up large amounts of blood, severe breathlessness, or high fever with confusion in a known
or suspected TB patient requires urgent referral to a hospital.

title: Suspected malaria
text:
Fever with chills and sweating, often cyclical, especially in a malaria-endemic area, should be
tested for malaria at the earliest opportunity. Refer for prompt testing and treatment; delayed
treatment risks progression to severe malaria (confusion, convulsions, severe anemia, jaundice),
which is a medical emergency.

title: Suspected dengue
text:
High fever with severe headache, pain behind the eyes, joint/muscle pain, and rash should raise
suspicion of dengue. Warning signs requiring immediate referral include: severe abdominal pain,
persistent vomiting, bleeding from gums/nose, black stools, restlessness, or cold/clammy skin —
these indicate possible dengue hemorrhagic complications.

title: Suspected chikungunya
text:
High fever with severe joint pain and swelling, often affecting hands, wrists, ankles, and feet, is
typical of chikungunya. It is rarely life-threatening but can cause prolonged joint pain; supportive
care with rest, fluids, and monitoring is generally appropriate, with referral if fever is very high
or persistent beyond a few days.

title: General prevention advice
text:
Advise use of mosquito nets, elimination of standing water near the home, and use of repellents
where available, regardless of which specific illness is suspected.
